Macrons

Theme

School & learning · Conversation, family & daily routines

read aloud verb

also read out, read out loud, read to someone

classical

Plaut. Pers. 500: at clārē recitātō
Cic. Att. 8.9.2 (Lewis & Short)
Traupman 27, 34

recitō, recitāre, recitāvī, recitātum

verb, first conjugation

read aloud, read out

To read a text out to listeners: a letter, a law, a list, one’s own poems; clārē, out loud. Under the Empire authors read their new works to invited audiences, the recitātiōnēs of Pliny’s letters (Lewis & Short).

Examples

  • Cedo sānē mihi. — At clārē recitātō. — Tacē, dum pellegō.

    Give it here, then. — But read it out loud. — Quiet, while I read it through.Plaut. Pers. 500

  • ōrātiōnem Graecam Latīnamve clārē et intentē nōn tam vōcis causā quam stomachī legō

    I read a speech, Greek or Latin, aloud and with effort, not so much for my voice’s sake as for my digestion’sPlin. Ep. 9.36.3

Other words

  • clārē legere — read out loud

    also used · classical · Plin. Ep. 9.36.3: clārē et intentē … legō; Traupman 34: lege clārē

  • praelegō, praelegere, praelēgī, praelēctum — read aloud to a class, read with explanations

    verb, third conjugation · also used · classical · Quint. 1.5.11 (Lewis & Short); Suet. Gram. 16: Vergilium et aliōs poētās (Lewis & Short)

    The teacher’s reading, to show how a text should be read and to explain it; Lewis & Short: post-Augustan. The reading is praelēctiō (see lecture).

See also read, recite, book, lesson, lecture.

SourcesLewis & Short: recito · Lewis & Short: clare · Lewis & Short: praelego
